---
title: "Exercise 5.2 — Hyperparameters: choosing the lasso and ridge penalty (with solutions)"
output: html_document
---

*HDS MSc · Module 3 · the R version of this exercise; the web page is at <https://inflamuob.github.io/HDS_M3/day5/day5-02-regularisation.html>.*

*Open it in RStudio and run it a chunk at a time. Keep it in the folder that holds your `data` folder. This version has the worked answers filled in.*

Some settings of a model are not learnt from the data: we choose them before
fitting. They are called **hyperparameters**. In this exercise the
hyperparameters are those of **regularisation**: a linear regression that pays
a price for large coefficients, so that it fits the training rows a little less
closely in exchange for a simpler model. How large the price is, $\lambda$,
must be chosen, and we choose it by trying several values and keeping the one
that predicts best on rows the model has not seen. The page
[Lasso and ridge in a picture](day5-01b-lasso-ridge-picture.qmd) explains what
the penalty does.

**Theory:** hyperparameters; a validation set; the lasso and ridge penalties;
grid search, random search and zooming in; refitting the chosen model and
checking it once on the test rows.

> **The plots are for looking at**
>
> The code for every plot is included, so that you can run it and see the figure. You are not expected to write it yourself.

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "glmnet"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 4)     # show four significant figures in tables
```

The same 750 people and the same split as Exercise 5.1, from
[`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv). The outcome is glucose
again, but this time the other seven measurements are the predictors. In
`pressure`, `triceps` and `insulin` a zero means "not measured", so we turn the
zeros into `NA` and let the recipe fill them in.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(-diabetes) |>                                          # glucose is the outcome
  mutate(across(c(pressure, triceps, insulin), ~ na_if(.x, 0)))  # 0 means "not measured"

test_rows <- seq(1, nrow(diabetes), by = 5)     # every fifth person is held back
train <- diabetes[-test_rows, ]
test  <- diabetes[test_rows, ]
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — A validation set

The test rows are for one final check of the model we choose. If we also use
them to *make* the choice, we pick whichever candidate happened to do best on
those 150 people, and its test RMSE is no longer an honest estimate (the
Stretch of Exercise 5.1). So we split the training rows once more. Every fourth
training row becomes a **validation** row: the candidates are fitted on the
other rows and compared on these.

```{r}
val_rows   <- seq(1, nrow(train), by = 4)       # every fourth training row
fitting    <- train[-val_rows, ]
validation <- train[val_rows, ]

nrow(fitting)
nrow(validation)
nrow(test)
```

450 rows to fit each candidate, 150 to compare the candidates, and 150 for the
final check.

> **Coming later: cross-validation**
>
> One validation set is the simplest way to compare candidates, but the result
> depends on which 150 people landed in it. In Exercise 5.4 you will learn
> **cross-validation**, a resampling method that repeats the comparison on
> several different splits of the training rows, and the functions that run the
> whole search for you.

Now a model with plenty of room to overfit. The recipe fills in the missing
values with the median (Day 2), adds every product of two predictors
(`pregnant_x_age`, …) and every square, and standardises the result. Seven
predictors become 35 columns.

```{r}
glucose_rec <- recipe(glucose ~ ., data = fitting) |>
  step_impute_median(all_predictors()) |>                        # fill the missing values
  step_interact(terms = ~ all_predictors():all_predictors()) |>  # products of two predictors
  step_poly(all_predictors(), -contains("_x_"), degree = 2,
            options = list(raw = TRUE)) |>                       # each predictor and its square
  step_normalize(all_predictors())                               # one scale for every column

glucose_rec |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  dim()
```

450 rows and 36 columns: glucose and the 35 predictor columns. Fit an
ordinary linear regression, with no penalty, and compare its RMSE on the
fitting and the validation rows:

```{r}
plain_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(glucose_rec) |>
  add_model(linear_reg()) |>
  fit(data = fitting)

augment(plain_fit, new_data = fitting) |>
  rmse(truth = glucose, estimate = .pred)
augment(plain_fit, new_data = validation) |>
  rmse(truth = glucose, estimate = .pred)
```

26.06 on the rows it was fitted on, 30.32 on the validation rows: the 35
columns have been used to fit some of the noise in the 450 people.

> **Learning points**
>
> - A **hyperparameter** is a setting we choose before fitting; the fitting does not choose it for us. The degree of the polynomial in Exercise 5.1 was one.
> - Candidates are compared on validation rows that were not used to fit them. The test rows are kept for one final check.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — One hyperparameter: a simple grid search

The lasso adds a penalty $\lambda \times \sum_j |\beta_j|$ to the fitting (see
[Lasso and ridge in a picture](day5-01b-lasso-ridge-picture.qmd)). $\lambda$ is
the hyperparameter: in tidymodels it is called `penalty`, and `mixture = 1`
asks for the lasso. We mark `penalty` with `tune()`, a placeholder for "to be
chosen", and fill it in later with `finalize_workflow()`:

```{r}
lasso_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(glucose_rec) |>
  add_model(linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) |>
              set_engine("glmnet"))
```

A **grid search** tries a list of values, fits one model for each, and keeps
the one with the lowest validation RMSE. Seven penalties, each about three
times the one before:

> **Stuck?**
>
> The candidates are compared on the rows that were **not** used to fit them.

> **Worked answer**

```{r}
penalties <- c(0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10)
lasso_results <- data.frame()

for (p in penalties) {
  lasso_fit <- lasso_wf |>
    finalize_workflow(tibble(penalty = p)) |>     # fill in the placeholder
    fit(data = fitting)

  fit_rmse <- augment(lasso_fit, new_data = fitting) |>
    rmse(truth = glucose, estimate = .pred)
  val_rmse <- augment(lasso_fit, new_data = validation) |>
    rmse(truth = glucose, estimate = .pred)
  kept <- tidy(lasso_fit) |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)", estimate != 0) |>
    nrow()                                         # columns the lasso kept

  lasso_results <- bind_rows(lasso_results,
                             data.frame(penalty  = p,
                                        fit_rmse = fit_rmse$.estimate,
                                        val_rmse = val_rmse$.estimate,
                                        kept     = kept))
}

lasso_results
```

```{r}
lasso_results |>
  pivot_longer(c(fit_rmse, val_rmse), names_to = "rows", values_to = "rmse") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = penalty, y = rmse, colour = rows)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Penalty (log scale)", y = "RMSE (mg/dL)", colour = NULL,
       title = "The lasso: fitting and validation RMSE for each penalty")
```

Read the table from top to bottom. The fitting RMSE only ever goes up: a
larger penalty always fits the fitting rows less closely. The validation RMSE
first falls, from 30.24 to its lowest value, 29.74 at a penalty of 0.3, and then
rises again, to 31.85 at 10. The penalty 0.3 is chosen because it has the
lowest validation RMSE, and at that penalty the lasso keeps 14 of the 35
columns.

**Question!** Why not choose the penalty with the lowest *fitting* RMSE?

> **Learning points**
>
> - A grid search fits one model for each candidate value and keeps the candidate with the lowest validation error.
> - Too small a penalty overfits, too large a penalty underfits; the validation error is lowest in between.
> - The fitting error always prefers the smallest penalty, so it cannot be used to choose.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — Two hyperparameters: a grid of combinations

`mixture` is a second hyperparameter: 1 is the lasso, 0 is ridge, and values in
between mix the two penalties. Mark both with `tune()`:

```{r}
enet_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(glucose_rec) |>
  add_model(linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) |>
              set_engine("glmnet"))
```

With two hyperparameters a grid search tries every **combination**.
`grid_regular()` builds the grid: 7 penalties from 0.01 to 10 (the range is
given on the log10 scale) and 5 mixtures from 0 to 1, so 7 × 5 = 35
combinations.

```{r}
regular_grid <- grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-2, 1)),
                             mixture(),
                             levels = c(penalty = 7, mixture = 5))
regular_grid
```

Fitting and scoring a candidate is the same few lines every time, so we put
them in a function and call it once for each row of the grid:

```{r}
validation_rmse <- function(penalty, mixture) {
  fitted <- enet_wf |>
    finalize_workflow(tibble(penalty = penalty, mixture = mixture)) |>
    fit(data = fitting)
  augment(fitted, new_data = validation) |>
    rmse(truth = glucose, estimate = .pred) |>
    pull(.estimate)
}

regular_grid$val_rmse <- NA
for (i in 1:nrow(regular_grid)) {
  regular_grid$val_rmse[i] <- validation_rmse(regular_grid$penalty[i],
                                              regular_grid$mixture[i])
}

regular_grid |>
  arrange(val_rmse) |>
  head(5)
```

```{r}
ggplot(regular_grid, aes(x = factor(signif(penalty, 2)), y = factor(mixture),
                         fill = val_rmse)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(val_rmse, 2)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(direction = -1) +
  labs(x = "Penalty", y = "Mixture (0 = ridge, 1 = lasso)", fill = "Validation\nRMSE",
       title = "Grid search: validation RMSE of each combination")
```

The best combination is a penalty of 0.32 with a mixture of 0.5, at 29.58: a
little better than the best lasso of Part 2 (29.74). Most of the grid lies
between 29.6 and 30.4; only the largest penalty is clearly worse.

> **Learning points**
>
> - With several hyperparameters, a grid search tries every combination, so the number of fits multiplies: 7 × 5 = 35 here.
> - `tune()` marks a hyperparameter to be chosen; `finalize_workflow()` fills in a value.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 4 — Other ways to search

A grid is not the only way to choose the candidates. **Random search** draws
the same number of combinations at random from the same ranges:

```{r}
set.seed(123)
random_grid <- grid_random(penalty(range = c(-2, 1)),
                           mixture(),
                           size = 35)

random_grid$val_rmse <- NA
for (i in 1:nrow(random_grid)) {
  random_grid$val_rmse[i] <- validation_rmse(random_grid$penalty[i],
                                             random_grid$mixture[i])
}

random_grid |>
  arrange(val_rmse) |>
  head(5)
```

```{r}
bind_rows(mutate(regular_grid, search = "grid search"),
          mutate(random_grid,  search = "random search")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = penalty, y = mixture, colour = val_rmse)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(direction = -1) +
  facet_wrap(~ search) +
  labs(x = "Penalty (log scale)", y = "Mixture", colour = "Validation\nRMSE",
       title = "The same 35 fits, placed two ways")
```

The random search finds 29.60 (penalty 0.38, mixture 0.41), as good as the grid
for the same 35 fits. Look at the plot: the grid tries only 7 different
penalties, the random search 35. When one hyperparameter matters much more than
the other, as the penalty does here, random search explores it more finely.

A third way is to **zoom in**: start with a coarse grid, then search a finer
grid around the best combination. Build a 5 × 5 grid with penalties from 0.1 to
1 and mixtures from 0.25 to 0.75 around the best of Part 3, and score it:

> **Stuck?**
>
> The range is on the log10 scale: $\log_{10}(0.1) = -1$ and $\log_{10}(1) = 0$.

> **Worked answer**

```{r}
fine_grid <- grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-1, 0)),   # log10 of 0.1 and of 1
                          mixture(range = c(0.25, 0.75)),
                          levels = c(penalty = 5, mixture = 5))

fine_grid$val_rmse <- NA
for (i in 1:nrow(fine_grid)) {
  fine_grid$val_rmse[i] <- validation_rmse(fine_grid$penalty[i],
                                           fine_grid$mixture[i])
}

fine_grid |>
  arrange(val_rmse) |>
  head(5)
```

> The finer grid finds nothing better: its best is the same combination as in
> Part 3 (penalty 0.32, mixture 0.5, 29.58), and its nearest rivals are within
> 0.06 of it. The coarse grid had already landed at the bottom.

There are cleverer searches still, which choose each new candidate using the
results so far, but they all work the same way: propose candidates, score each
on data the model was not fitted on, keep the best.

> **Learning points**
>
> - Grid search, random search and zooming in differ only in **which** candidates they try; each candidate is scored the same way.
> - For the same number of fits, random search tries more distinct values of each hyperparameter.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 5 — The final model and its one test

Take the best candidate of all the searches. Fit it once more, now on all 600
training rows (fitting and validation together), and check it once on the test
rows. Do the same for the unpenalised model, to compare:

> **Stuck?**
>
> Both models are fitted on the same rows, and both are checked on the rows that
> were held back from the start.

> **Worked answer**

```{r}
best <- bind_rows(regular_grid, random_grid, fine_grid) |>
  slice_min(val_rmse, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)   # the lowest; one row even if tied
best

final_fit <- enet_wf |>
  finalize_workflow(best |> select(penalty, mixture)) |>
  fit(data = train)

plain_final <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(glucose_rec) |>
  add_model(linear_reg()) |>
  fit(data = train)

augment(final_fit, new_data = test) |>
  rmse(truth = glucose, estimate = .pred)
augment(plain_final, new_data = test) |>
  rmse(truth = glucose, estimate = .pred)
```

> The chosen model (penalty 0.32, mixture 0.5) has a test RMSE of 26.90 against
> 27.12 for the unpenalised model, and it uses 19 of the 35 columns. Count them
> with `tidy(final_fit) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)", estimate != 0) |> nrow()`.

**Question!** The penalised model is only a little more accurate on the test
rows, but it uses about half the columns. Why might that still matter?

> **Learning points**
>
> - Once the hyperparameters are chosen, refit on all the training rows and check the model once on the test rows.
> - The test rows played no part in any choice, so the test RMSE is an honest estimate for new people.

## Stretch

> **Stretch — a different validation set**
>
> Make the validation rows every fourth training row starting from the second
> (`seq(2, nrow(train), by = 4)` in R, `np.arange(len(train)) % 4 == 1` in
> Python) and run the lasso grid of Part 2 again. Is the same penalty chosen?
> What does that tell you about choosing with a single validation set?
